r:
This traces block device I/O (disk I/O), and prints ratio of random/sequential I/O for each disk or the specified disk either on Ctrl-C, or after a given interval in seconds.

This works by tracing kernel tracepoint block:block_rq_complete.

Since this uses BPF, only the root user can use this tool.

<dl><dt data-o="">-h</dt><dd>Show help message and exit.</dd><dt data-o="">-d</dt><dd>Trace this disk only.</dd><dt>interval</dt><dd>Print output every interval seconds, if any.</dd><dt>count</dt><dd>Number of interval summaries.</dd></dl>

Trace access patterns of all disks, and print a summary on Ctrl-C:
# biopattern
Trace disk sdb only:
# biopattern -d sdb
Print 1 second summaries, 10 times:
# biopattern 1 10

<dl><dt>TIME</dt><dd>Time of the output, in HH:MM:SS format.</dd><dt>DISK</dt><dd>Disk device name.</dd><dt>%RND</dt><dd>Ratio of random I/O.</dd><dt>%SEQ</dt><dd>Ratio of sequential I/O.</dd><dt>COUNT</dt><dd>Number of I/O during the interval.</dd><dt>KBYTES</dt><dd>Total Kbytes for these I/O, during the interval.</dd></dl>

Since block device I/O usually has a relatively low frequency (< 10,000/s), the overhead for this tool is expected to be low or negligible. For high IOPS storage systems, test and quantify before use.

This is from bcc.

https://github.com/iovisor/bcc

Also look in the bcc distribution for a companion _examples.txt file containing example usage, output, and commentary for this tool.
